transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-06-30
Time: 15:00 PT (45 minutes)
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Lena Cho (Stellar PM), Ravi Singh (Stellar ML), Aisha Gomez (Stellar CTO)

[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check — is this still a good time for 45 minutes?
[00:06] Lena Cho: Yep, all good here.
[00:10] Diego Ramos: Hi all, Diego from Redwood. I'll mostly cover the regression numbers and the bench setup.
[00:15] Ravi Singh: Morning, or afternoon, yeah thanks.
[00:20] Maya Patel: Cool. Agenda: quick recap, go through the latest quality evals we ran on your prompt sets, dig into the regression we flagged on the insurance-explainer set, and agree next steps.

[02:12] Diego Ramos: Okay jumping in — we ran the baseline and the tuned prompt set across the 3k eval cases you provided. High-level: semantic similarity avg went from 0.76 to 0.78, ROUGE-L median improved from 0.59 to 0.63, so small gains overall. But hallucination rate edged up from 4.5% to 8% on the insurance-explainer slice specifically.

[02:45] Ravi Singh: Wait 8%? That's concerning — our target was <5% for that slice. Any idea what's driving the spike?

[03:02] Diego Ramos: We dug into the logs. Two things: the tuned system prompt added a few examples that are borderline leading the model to be overly speculative on policy details, and there was a change in stop-sequence usage — we used a softer stop which sometimes lets the model keep going and invent specifics.

[03:38] Lena Cho: That matches what we saw; some outputs had made-up policy numbers and named forms that don't exist. We logged them as hallucinations.

[04:05] Maya Patel: Yep — so root cause looks like prompt examples + softer stops. Diego, did you check temperature settings?

[04:18] Diego Ramos: Good call. We kept temperature at 0.2 for the tuned run to preserve variability, previous baseline was 0.0 — so that contributes. Also k-vee cache behavior — sorry, KV cache — the cache hit pattern changed slightly because of the added few-shot examples, which might change token conditioning for some inputs.

[04:45] Ravi Singh: "K-vee cache" — ha, classic transcription. But yes, we suspected changes in conditioning.

[05:10] Aisha Gomez: From an engineering standpoint, latency is still fine on hosted, but we need to understand if Dedicated will help reduce variance and whether quantized model variants introduce new regressions.

[05:30] Diego Ramos: For Dedicated we can pin a model variant (e.g., 8-bit quant) and run the same harness. Typically quantization reduces latency and can slightly nudge outputs; we saw minimal semantic drift in previous tests, but it's worth validating.

[06:05] Lena Cho: Can you remind us of the eval scoring approach you used? There's sometimes confusion between semantic-similarity thresholds and human pass/fail.

[06:18] Diego Ramos: Sure. We used a hybrid scoring: automatic semantic similarity (embedding cosine) as primary numeric metric, ROUGE-L as lexical sanity-check, and a human label pass/fail for the 500-case stratified sample. The regression threshold we set was: if hallucination rate increases by >2% absolute or semantic similarity drops by >0.03, we flag.

[06:46] Ravi Singh: And for semantic similarity, what's the threshold for acceptable?

[06:50] Diego Ramos: We use 0.7 as a loose target for the feature you care about; critical slices (e.g., policy explanations) we want >0.75 and hallucinations <5%.

[07:08] Lena Cho: Okay that aligns. The insurance-explainer slice dropped to 0.68 on a subset when hallucinations happen.

[07:20] Maya Patel: So concrete options: 1) revert the few-shot examples in the system prompt, 2) decrease temperature to 0.0-0.1 for that route, 3) enforce a hard stop or token-limit guardrail, 4) add post-generation filtering and a hallucination detector threshold that triggers a fallback response or escalate to 'unable to answer' template.

[07:50] Ravi Singh: I like the hallucination detector idea. Do you have a recommended similarity threshold that indicates probable hallucination?

[07:58] Diego Ramos: From our last experiments, if the top-k answer similarity to the reference doc embeddings is <0.55 it's high risk. Combined with heuristics (presence of numeric policy identifiers not in the KB) we can flag.

[08:20] Lena Cho: Would that be a trainable classifier or heuristic? We have some label budget but not a ton.

[08:28] Diego Ramos: Start with heuristics plus embedding thresholds; we can then add a small supervised classifier if you provide labeled hallucination examples. That classifier can run in the post-process step on Redwood's serving or on your side.

[09:05] Aisha Gomez: Any quick wins we can test this week?

[09:12] Maya Patel: Yes — Diego can run the harness with the tuned prompt but with temperature 0.0 and hard stop, and also run the post-filter. If hallucination drops back under 5% and semantic similarity stays acceptable, we can keep the tuning.

[09:35] Diego Ramos: I'll run three variants: (A) tuned prompt + temp 0.2 (current), (B) tuned prompt + temp 0.0 + hard stop, (C) tuned prompt without few-shot examples + temp 0.0. I'll capture ROUGE, semantic sim, hallucination rate, and a sample of 200 human-reviewed cases for bias.

[10:02] Ravi Singh: Great. Also we want to understand any regressions introduced by quantized variants — can we add a DQ test?

[10:10] Diego Ramos: Yes, we'll include a quantized run on Dedicated-like hardware. For the bench we'll measure p50/p95 latency, tokens/sec, and cost per 1k tokens.

[10:25] Lena Cho: On reporting format — please put the scoring sheet in the same Google Sheet as before, add a column for 'regression reason' (prompt, temp, stop, quantization).

[10:35] Maya Patel: Absolutely. We'll also mark examples flagged by the hallucination detector.

[11:05] Maya Patel: A couple of security questions came in from Aisha earlier — VPC/private deployment notes and KMS keys. We will share SOC2 excerpts and our KMS integration doc after the call.

[11:20] Aisha Gomez: Thanks, we need that for procurement. Also curious about logging retention and PII redaction — any defaults?

[11:30] Diego Ramos: Hosted defaults retain logs for 30 days but for Dedicated/Private we can configure retention and integrate with your KMS/HSM for encryption. We also offer a PII redaction pre-processing filter and audit logs. We'll send the detailed doc.

[12:02] Ravi Singh: Back to quality — can we map a failure-case priority? For example, hallucinations that mention specific policy numbers cause compliance risk and should be P0, while incomplete answers can be P2.

[12:20] Lena Cho: Yes, let's do that. We'll attach a priority column in the shared sheet.

[12:38] Diego Ramos: Quick note — some transcriptions and names may look off in the logs; the transcript generator mislabels speaker a bit. Ignore "k-vee" in the raw logs.

[13:05] Maya Patel: Next steps recap: Diego to run the three variant regression runs and a quantized Dedicated run, share the updated scoring sheet; Maya to share security docs and the prompt variants; Stellar to deliver 200 labeled examples and confirm stakeholders. We'll reconvene after you review the regression spreadsheet.

[13:40] Lena Cho: Sounds good. Targeting a follow-up sync after the spreadsheet — maybe July 7?

[13:50] Maya Patel: July 7 works — we'll propose times.

[14:05] Aisha Gomez: One last question — if we keep hallucination detector and fallback, how will that affect UX? Will users see more 'I don't know' responses?

[14:18] Diego Ramos: Potentially yes, but we can craft fallback templates that prompt escalation: "I don't have verified info right now — would you like me to connect you with support or show docs?" That keeps UX acceptable while avoiding bad policy fabrications.

[14:40] Ravi Singh: Ok good. I think we have a plan.

[44:30] Maya Patel: Thanks everyone — we'll send notes and the links out right after.

[44:40] Lena Cho: Thanks all.

[45:00] End of recording
